title: Why do work emails take so long to write? Causes, costs and Mac fixes for developers
metaTitle: Why Work Emails Take So Long to Write: Mac Fixes for 2026
description: Work emails take long because you reread threads, start from a blank page, and rewrite for tone. Here are the costs, causes and Mac fixes.
targetKeyword: why do work emails take so long to write
secondaryKeywords: how to write work emails faster
reduce time spent writing work emails
intro: Work emails take long because you reread the thread, stare at a blank page, and rewrite for tone. Each step costs a few minutes, and they add up across a week. This page covers what it costs, why it happens, and fixes you can use on your Mac today.
tldr: Long work emails usually come from three things: reading the thread, drafting from a blank page, and rewriting for tone.
Microsoft's 2023 data puts the heaviest 25% of email users at 8.8 hours a week. Your own number may differ, so measure it.
At 5 hours a week and a $38.00 average hourly rate, the cost is about $9,120 a year. That is our arithmetic, not a survey.
Only the checking limit has study support here. Text Replacements, Writing Tools, fixed checking times, and scheduled sends are practical but untested.
Lazur can answer questions about a thread out loud and dictate or draft text. It does not send your email for you.

blocks.text: What the research says about email time

Good data on work email time is thin. The most useful figure comes from Microsoft's 2023 Work Trend Index. It says the heaviest 25% of email users spend 8.8 hours a week on email. The survey covered 31,000 full-time employed or self-employed workers in 31 markets. Microsoft 365 usage data came from a rolling 28-day period ending March 2023.
Read that number as a warning sign, not a benchmark. Heavy users are not average users. The figure shows what the top of the range looks like, and that is useful when you compare your own week.

Microsoft's June 2025 follow-up gives a different view. The average worker receives 117 emails a day, and most get skimmed in under 60 seconds. That is a reading figure. It does not report weekly hours on email, so it cannot tell you how long writing takes.

The same follow-up says employees are interrupted 275 times a day. That count covers only the top 20% of users by ping volume. Do not treat it as your own number. Use it to see how loud a busy inbox can get.

The 2023 report also splits your Microsoft 365 time by type of work. Email makes up 15% of that time. Communicating, which covers meetings, email, and chat, takes 57%. Creating takes 43%. Communication takes more of that time than creating does.
What a slow email habit costs you each week

Start with hours, then turn hours into money. Count the minutes you spend reading threads, drafting, and rereading. Do this for one normal week. A rough number is enough to decide whether a fix is worth an afternoon.

Here is the math, with the inputs labeled. The BLS puts average hourly earnings for all private-sector employees at $38.00 in its October 2026 release. That is a broad average, not a pay rate. Five hours a week over 48 working weeks comes to 240 hours, or about $9,120 a year. The five hours and the 48 weeks are example inputs. Replace them with your own.

blocks.caption: Our arithmetic from the BLS rate. Not a survey figure.

blocks.text: The money is only part of the cost. Email also breaks your focus. Kushlev and Dunn tested checking habits directly. Their study enrolled 124 adults, about two-thirds of them students, in a two-week design.

In one week, people checked email three times a day. In the other week, they checked without a limit. Daily stress was lower in the limited week, though most people found the limit hard to keep. UBC's summary gives no effect sizes, so do not promise a number.
Why work emails take so long to write

Most slow emails are slow before the first word. You open the thread and scroll for the question. You check a ticket, a pull request, or a Slack message. By the time you type, you have already spent part of the job rebuilding context.

The second delay is the blank page. A reply to a product manager about a slipped release has many possible openings. You type one, delete it, and type another. Each restart costs more than the sentence itself.
Developers feel this most with bad news. The message must explain a cause, give a date, and avoid sounding defensive. Several goals at once make every sentence slower to write.
Mistakes that make the problem worse

items: Rewriting the same paragraph again and again. Each pass adds length, and the tone rarely gets clearer.
Checking the inbox every few minutes. Each check restarts your focus before you finish the reply.
Writing every reply from scratch. Most work replies repeat the same few answers.
Replying to the whole thread in one message. The reader then has to find the answer again.
Leaving email for the end of the day. Replies arrive late, and the work after them stalls.

blocks.text: Every mistake on that list has a cheap fix. The next sections cover the ones that take minutes to set up, then the ones that need a habit change.
Set up Text Replacements for the replies you send every week

Text Replacements turn a short trigger into a full sentence or paragraph. Developers often send the same few messages, such as a deploy status, a request for a call, or a reproduction request. Store them once and reuse them.

items: Choose Apple menu > System Settings > Keyboard > Text Replacements.
Click Add. Type the short trigger, then the full text it should expand into.
Click Done. Apple says Text Replacements are not available in all apps, so test them in each app you use.

blocks.title: Pick triggers you will not type by accident
blocks.text: Use a prefix that ordinary words never start with, such as //deploy. A common word as a trigger will fire in the middle of normal sentences.
Let Writing Tools proofread and rewrite your draft

Writing Tools works on text you have already written. Select the text, Control-click it, then choose Writing Tools > Show Writing Tools. The menu offers Proofread, Rewrite with Friendly, Professional, or Concise, Summarize or Key Points, and Describe a change.
Use Rewrite with Concise on a long draft. Then read the output against the thread. The tool changes wording. It cannot know whether the release really moved to a new date.

Check your version before you plan around it. Apple's Mac Help page for Writing Tools covers macOS 27. Apple also says Apple Intelligence is not available in every language or region, and usage limits may apply. Compose needs the ChatGPT extension. I did not verify older macOS versions.

blocks.title: Read every rewrite
blocks.text: A rewrite can soften a deadline or drop a date. Compare the output with the thread before you paste it. Keep the facts in your own hands.
Batch your email checks into fixed windows

Checking less is the one habit in this page with study support. Kushlev and Dunn's paper, published in Computers in Human Behavior, tested a limit of three checks a day. People felt less stressed in the limited week.

Most people found the limit hard to keep, so make it concrete. Pick fixed times, such as the start of the day, after lunch, and before you stop. Turn off Mail banner alerts in System Settings so new messages wait for your window.
Schedule sends and summarize threads in Gmail and Outlook

In Gmail on a computer, click Compose. Click the down arrow next to Send, then choose Schedule send. Gmail lets you keep up to 100 scheduled emails. Scheduled emails may go out a few minutes late, so keep exact times out of it.
Scheduling helps with time zones. Write the reply while the thread is fresh, then send it at the start of the other person's day. You avoid a second writing session later.

In Outlook for Mac, open the message and click the Copilot icon on the message toolbar. Choose Summarize and reply to this email. Microsoft says Copilot in Outlook works only in the latest Outlook for Mac. Legacy Outlook is not supported.

blocks.text: A worked example: a status email after a slipped release
Say a release slipped because of a bad migration. The client wants the new date, the cause, and what changes. The thread is long, so you start by reading it, not typing.
Ask before you reread. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask what the client asked for in the last message. Lazur answers out loud. Keep the thread open and check the key lines yourself.

Dictate the first pass next. Click in the reply, hold fn, and speak in plain words. Say the cause in one sentence and the new date in full. Dictation types the text at the cursor, so you can edit it right away.

Then run Writing Tools > Rewrite with Concise on the draft. Compare the new date with the thread. If the rewrite changed a fact, put the original back. Proofread last. If the client sits in another time zone, use Schedule send for their morning.
Handle sensitive email with care

Not every email can go into an AI tool. If you handle client data, personal data, or security details, follow your employer rules first. Developers face this too. Customer records, API keys, and incident details can sit in the thread you are rewriting.

blocks.title: Regulated work needs employer rules
blocks.text: If you work as a lawyer, nurse, or accountant, follow your employer rules on client or patient data before you use any AI tool on that text.

Here is what Lazur does with your input. It listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so they can answer. They are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models. Your employer may still say no, and that rule wins.
What to change first and how to measure it

Change one thing for a week. Start with Text Replacements because it takes minutes to set up. Add scheduled sends for messages that can wait. Keep a note of the minutes you spend on email each day, then compare it with your first week.

Be honest about the evidence. The checking limit has study support. The Microsoft figures come from Microsoft 365 usage, not a random sample of all workers. The 2025 telemetry also excludes education and EU tenants. Writing Tools, templates, and scheduled sends are practical, but no source here shows they cut writing time.

If your slowest emails are about code, start with the thread. Ask Lazur to explain the thread out loud before you open the reply box. For more on protecting focus between messages, read [how to recover focus after interruptions while coding on Mac](/for/developers/problems/developer-context-switching-recovery-time). For dictation in developer tools, see [AI dictation for developers](/blog/ai-dictation-for-developers).

faq.question: Why do work emails take so long to write for most people?
faq.answer: Usually the delay comes before the first word. You reread the thread, find the question, and check the facts. Then you draft from a blank page and rewrite for tone. Each step is small, but together they fill the afternoon.

faq.question: How much time do work emails take each week?
faq.answer: Microsoft's 2023 data says the heaviest 25% of email users spend 8.8 hours a week on email. That figure covers reading and writing together, not writing alone. Measure one normal week of your own time to get a real number.

faq.question: Does checking email less really lower stress?
faq.answer: A study of 124 adults found less daily stress in a week of checking email three times a day, compared with a week of unlimited checking. Most participants found the limit hard to keep. UBC's summary gives no effect sizes.

faq.question: Can Writing Tools write my emails from scratch?
faq.answer: Writing Tools proofreads, rewrites, and summarizes text you have already written. Compose, which writes new text, works through the ChatGPT extension. Read every output, check the facts, and send it yourself.

faq.question: Does Lazur send my email for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons or operate other apps for you. It can draft text, dictate at the cursor, and guide you one click at a time. You read the message and press Send.

faq.question: Is it safe to paste client emails into an AI tool?
faq.answer: Follow your employer rules first, especially for client, patient, or personal data. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and screenshots go to AI providers, and they are not stored.

faq.question: Why did my scheduled Gmail email arrive late?
faq.answer: Google says scheduled emails may be sent a few minutes late. Do not use Schedule send for a message that must go out at an exact minute. Use it for timing that is roughly right, such as the start of a workday.

faq.question: Why is Outlook Copilot missing from my Outlook?
faq.answer: Microsoft says Copilot in Outlook works only in the latest Outlook for Mac, and legacy Outlook is not supported. I did not verify which license or plan it needs. Ask your admin or check Microsoft's support page.

costs.title: Hours each week
costs.text: Microsoft's 2023 data puts the heaviest 25% of email users at 8.8 hours a week. Most users fall below that line. The cost is still real if your week fills with threads. Measure your own week before you decide what to fix.

costs.title: Focus between messages
costs.text: Each check pulls you away from code, a review, or a design. The Kushlev and Dunn study tied fewer checks to lower daily stress. The gain came from checking less often, not from deleting mail. This cost shows up as broken concentration, which is harder to measure than minutes.

costs.title: Late replies
costs.text: A reply that waits until the end of the day holds up the person who asked. A developer who waits on a product answer may stall a ticket for hours. Slow replies cost the team time, even when your writing is quick.

costs.title: Rewrites that add length
costs.text: Rewriting a paragraph again and again feels careful. It often makes the message longer and vaguer. The extra passes cost minutes and make the reader work harder to find the point.

costs.title: Stress and workload
costs.text: Gallup's 2026 global report says 40% of employees felt a lot of stress the previous day. That figure covers stress in general, not email. Do not credit email with all of it. Still, inbox pressure is one part of a heavy day.

causes.title: The context lives in other tools
causes.text: Your answer depends on a Slack thread, a Linear ticket, a pull request, and a shared doc. Each one needs a tab and a careful read. Much of the delay comes from rebuilding that context before you type. Read the sources once, then write from your notes.

causes.title: Blank-page starts
causes.text: A blank reply has no shape. You try an opening, judge it, and delete it. Starting with a short list of the answers gives the message a shape before the tone questions begin.

causes.title: Tone worry on bad news
causes.text: Delays, bugs, and missed dates make people slow down. You want the message to be clear, calm, and not defensive. Those goals pull against each other. Extra checking makes the draft longer and the wait longer too.

causes.title: Constant interruption
causes.text: Each notification asks for a quick look. A quick look becomes a reply, then a second reply. Every switch between code and mail breaks the thread of your work. Frequent checks keep the inbox in control of your day.

causes.title: Replies written from scratch
causes.text: Many work replies repeat the same answers. Status updates, meeting requests, and reproduction steps show up every week. Writing them from scratch takes longer than pulling a saved version and editing one line.

causes.title: Threads that ask several questions
causes.text: A long thread often hides several questions in different messages. You must find each one, answer it, and check that none were missed. Pulling out the questions first saves a rewrite later.

causes.title: Long replies by default
causes.text: Long replies take longer to write and longer to read. Many people send the full story when the reader needs the answer and one next step. Leading with the answer shortens both sides of the exchange.

fixes.title: Store repeat replies as Text Replacements
fixes.text: Save the replies you send most often under short triggers. Start with one status update and one meeting request. Test each trigger in the apps you use, because Apple says Text Replacements are not available in all apps.

fixes.title: List the questions before you draft
fixes.text: Copy the thread's open questions into a short list in a note. Answer each line in order. This keeps the reply short and stops you from missing a question the sender asked.

fixes.title: Lead with the answer and the date
fixes.text: Put the answer or the new date in the first sentence. Put the cause after it, and the next step last. Readers often stop after the first line, so the top line does the most work.

fixes.title: Batch checks into fixed windows
fixes.text: Choose checking times and keep them. Turn off Mail banner alerts so new messages wait for your window. Study participants found a limit hard to keep, so write the times down where you can see them.

fixes.title: Proofread and tighten with Writing Tools
fixes.text: Select a finished draft. Use Proofread for typos and Rewrite with Concise for length, if your Mac supports Writing Tools. Read the rewrite against the thread, and put back any fact the tool changed.

fixes.title: Schedule sends for other time zones
fixes.text: In Gmail on a computer, click Compose, then the down arrow next to Send, then Schedule send. Use it to land a reply at the start of the other person's day, not at an exact minute.

fixes.title: Use a reply checklist before you send
fixes.text: Check each reply for the date, the owner, and the next step. Confirm that every question in the thread has an answer. A checklist takes seconds and prevents a second email that says you forgot something.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Measure one normal week
plan.text: Keep a note of the minutes you spend on email each day. Split the time into reading threads, drafting, and rereading. The note gives you a real starting number instead of a guess.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Set up Text Replacements
plan.text: Add the replies you send most, such as a status update and a meeting request. Test each trigger in Mail and Chrome. Apple says the feature is not available in all apps.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Pick fixed checking times
plan.text: Choose the start of the day, after lunch, and before you stop as your checking times. Turn off Mail banner alerts so new messages wait. Note how many urgent messages actually came in.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Try Writing Tools on one draft
plan.text: Write a reply the normal way. Select it, then use Proofread and Rewrite with Concise. Read each rewrite against the thread and keep the facts that matter.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Schedule one send and compare
plan.text: Use Schedule send in Gmail for a message to another time zone. Then compare your minutes from Day 1 with this week. Keep the fixes that saved time and drop the rest.
